implementation_notes: The default in-process realization: a std::queue guarded by std::mutex with a std::condition_variable waking one waiting worker per item, and N std::thread consumers that pop under the lock and process outside it. Only one thread can complete a pop, so the queue itself is the arbiter; a second condition variable (not_full) adds the capacity bound that std::queue lacks.
pitfalls: Condition-variable waits must loop on the predicate; a missed notification otherwise parks workers with items still queued.
Processing inside the critical section serialises the pool - the dequeue must release the lock before the handler runs.
std::queue has no capacity, so the producer side grows memory without backpressure unless a not_full condition is added.

variants.name: std::jthread workers with cooperative stop
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 removes the shutdown boilerplate: std::jthread joins on destruction and carries a std::stop_token, so workers wait on condition_variable_any with the token's stop callback and the pool stops without a hand-rolled 'stopping' flag and last-worker notification. The competing-consumer mechanics are unchanged - one mutex-guarded queue, N threads - but lifetime management moves into the language.
pitfalls: Forget to pass the stop_token into the wait and a stopped pool finishes its current item but never exits the loop.
A jthread that owns the queue must outlive it: member declaration order decides destruction order, and stopping after the queue is gone is undefined behaviour.

variants.name: ZeroMQ PULL workers (broker in the socket)
variants.idiom_name: ZeroMQ PULL workers (broker in the socket)
variants.implementation_notes: When the competing consumers are processes rather than threads, ZeroMQ supplies the queue as a socket type: PUSH producers bind and N PULL workers connect, and libzmq distributes each message to exactly one connected worker (fair-queuing), which is the pattern across processes and hosts without writing a broker or a lock. The trade-off is an external dependency and its own failure model - no persistence, no acknowledgement, no redelivery.
pitfalls: PUSH/PULL has no acknowledgement or persistence: a worker that dies after recv loses the message unless the application adds an ack layer or a broker.
Fair-queuing only holds for connected peers - slow-joiner effects (a worker connecting late misses work) are a common surprise when scaling out.
